concepts.title: recurrence
concepts.one_liner: A feedback connection defines a recurrence in the computational graph.
concepts.content:
A feedback connection defines a **recurrence** in the computational graph.

Their computation graphs have cycles. That means that the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of **timestep**. One timestep of running an RNN corresponds to one functional call to each layer (or computation node) in the RNN, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Recurrence allows outputs of one layer to influence earlier layers, enabling RNNs to process sequences with feedback loops over time steps.
concepts.recap_md:
- A recurrence is defined by a feedback connection in the computational graph.
- Recurrence introduces cycles where outputs can feed back to earlier layers.
- RNNs use timesteps to make these cycles well-defined.

concepts.title: RNNs are all about adaptation
concepts.one_liner: RNNs are all about adaptation: they allow past computations to influence future computations.
concepts.content: RNNs are all about adaptation. They solve the following problem: What if we want our computations in the past to influence our computations in the future? If we have a stream of data, a feedforward net has no way to adapting its behavior based on what outputs it previously produced.
concepts.motivation_md: RNNs address the problem of adapting computations based on past outputs, which feedforward nets cannot do.
concepts.recap_md:
- RNNs enable adaptation over time.
- They allow past computations to influence future ones.
- Feedforward nets cannot adapt based on previous outputs.

concepts.title: Memory in RNNs via recurrent feedback loops
concepts.one_liner: The recurrent feedback loops in an RNN are a kind of memory, propagating information from timestep $t$ to $t+1$.
concepts.content: The answer is memory. The recurrent feedback loops in an RNN are a kind of memory. They propagate information from timestep $t$ to timestep $t+1$. In other words, they remember information about timestep $t$ when processing new information at timestep $t+1$. Thus, by induction, an RNN can potentially remember information over arbitrarily long time intervals. In fact, RNNs are Turing complete: you can think of them as a little computer. They can do anything a computer can do.

concepts.recap_md:

- They pass information from timestep $t$ to $t+1$.
- RNNs can remember information over arbitrarily long intervals and are Turing complete.

concepts.title: unrolled computation graph
concepts.one_liner: The unrolled computation graph is a DAG representation of an RNN's computation over time, making backpropagation applicable.
concepts.content:
(see figure: RNN with multidimensional inputs, hidden states, and outputs.)

To the left, is the **unrolled computation graph**. To the right, is the computation graph rolled up, with a feedback connection. Typically we will work with unrolled graphs because they are directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and therefore all the tools we have developed for DAGs, including backpropagation, will extend naturally to them. However, note that RNNs can run for unbounded time, and process signals that have unbounded temporal extent, while a DAG can only represent a finite graph. The DAG depicted above is therefore a *truncated* version of the RNN's theoretical computation graph.
concepts.motivation_md: Unrolling an RNN's computation graph removes cycles, enabling the use of DAG-based tools like backpropagation.
concepts.recap_md:
- The unrolled computation graph represents RNN computations as a DAG.
- DAGs allow use of backpropagation and other DAG tools.
- The unrolled graph is a truncated finite representation of the RNN's infinite computation.

concepts.title: Recurrent Layer
concepts.one_liner: A recurrent layer includes a state variable that updates every call, acting as a kind of memory.

- The output depends on the current state, providing memory.

concepts.title: The idea of time in an RNN
concepts.one_liner: Time in an RNN refers to sequential computation steps indexed by timestep $t$, not necessarily clock time.
concepts.content: The idea of a *time* in an RNN does not necessarily mean time as it is measured on a clock. Time just refers to *sequential computation*; the timestep $t$ is an index into the sequence. The sequential computation could progress over a spatial dimension (processing an image pixel by pixel) or over the temporal dimension (processing a video frame by frame), or even over more abstracted computational modules.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding 'time' as sequential steps allows RNNs to process data ordered by any sequence, not just clock time.
concepts.recap_md:
- Time in RNNs means sequential computation, not clock time.
- Timestep $t$ indexes the sequence.
- Sequence can be spatial, temporal, or abstract computational steps.

concepts.title: SRN
concepts.one_liner: An SRN is a recurrent layer where $f$ is a linear layer plus nonlinearity and $g$ is another linear layer.
concepts.content:
One common kind of recurrent layer is the (**SRN**), which was defined by Elman in "Finding Structure in Time" @elman1990finding. For this layer, $f$ is a linear layer followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, and $g$ is another linear layer. The full computation is defined by the following equations: 
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{h}_t &= \sigma_1(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]+ \mathbf{b})\\
    \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]&= \sigma_2(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c})
\end{aligned}$$ where $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are pointwise nonlinearities. In SRNs, tanh is the common choice for the nonlinearity, but relus and other choices may also be used.
concepts.motivation_md: The SRN is a foundational recurrent layer model combining linear transformations and nonlinearities to process sequential data.
concepts.recap_md:
- SRN is a recurrent layer defined by Elman.
- $f$ is a linear layer plus nonlinearity; $g$ is another linear layer.
- Common nonlinearities include tanh and relu.

concepts.title: output gate
concepts.one_liner: The output gate determines which indices of the cell state to use and how to compute the next hidden state.
concepts.motivation_md: The output gate controls which parts of the cell state influence the hidden state, enabling selective information flow in LSTMs.
concepts.recap_md:
- The output gate $\mathbf{o}_t$ is computed using the previous hidden state, current input, and biases.
- It determines which indices of the cell state $\mathbf{c}_t$ to use.
- The next hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$ is the elementwise product of $\mathbf{o}_t$ and $\tanh(\mathbf{c}_t)$.

\mathbf{h}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t \odot \texttt{tanh}(\mathbf{c}_t) &\triangleleft \quad\quad\text{use these to determine next hidden state}

concepts.title: recurrent connections and feedback
concepts.one_liner: Recurrent connections allow neural nets to maintain a persistent state and adapt based on feedback from downstream processing.
concepts.content: Recurrent connections give neural nets the ability to maintain a persistent state representation, which can be propagated forward in time or updated with incoming experience. This idea is analogous to the distinction between open-loop and closed-loop control in control theory. Closed-loop control allows the controller to change behavior based on feedback from the consequences of previous decisions. Similarly, recurrent connections allow a neural net to change behavior based on feedback from downstream processing within the same network. Feedback is a fundamental mechanism for making systems adaptive, enabling them to become more competent the longer they run.
concepts.motivation_md: Recurrent connections enable neural networks to adapt dynamically by using feedback, allowing them to maintain and update internal states over time for improved performance. (book-extracted)
concepts.recap_md:

- They enable feedback-based adaptation within the neural net.
- Feedback allows systems to become more competent with continued operation.

motivation.text: Feedback is a fundamental mechanism for making systems that are adaptive. These systems can become more competent the longer you run them.

concepts.title: Recurrent Neural Nets
concepts.one_liner: RNNs are neural nets with feedback connections that model sequences by performing sequential computation.
concepts.content:
RNNs are a neural net architecture for modeling sequences---they perform *sequential* computation (rather than parallel computation).

So far we have seen **feedforward** neural net architectures. These architectures can be represented by directed acyclical computation graphs. (**RNNs**), are neural nets with feedback connections. 

A feedback connection defines a **recurrence** in the computational graph.

Their computation graphs have cycles. That means that the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of **timestep**. One timestep of running an RNN corresponds to one functional call to each layer (or computation node) in the RNN, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: RNNs model sequential data by introducing feedback connections and timesteps, enabling the network to process sequences over time.
concepts.recap_md:
- RNNs perform sequential computation with feedback connections.
- They have cycles in their computation graphs.
- Timesteps define discrete processing steps mapping inputs to outputs.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through Time
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through time (BPTT) applies backpropagation to RNNs by unrolling the net for $T$ timesteps, creating a DAG representation for gradient computation.
concepts.content:
Backpropagation is only defined for directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), but recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are not DAGs. To apply backpropagation to RNNs, we unroll the network for $T$ timesteps, which creates a DAG representation of the truncated RNN, and then perform backpropagation through that DAG. This method is known as backpropagation through time (BPTT).

This approach yields exact gradients of the loss with respect to the parameters when $T$ equals the total number of timesteps the RNN was run for. Otherwise, BPTT approximates the true computation graph by truncating it, effectively ignoring any dependencies longer than $T$ timesteps.

For example, to compute the gradient of an output neuron at timestep five with respect to an input at timestep zero, i.e., $\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[5]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[0]}$, the forward pass (black arrows) and backward pass (red arrows) are illustrated in @fig-recurrent_neural_nets-bptt1, showing only the relevant subpart of the computation graph.

(see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN.)

Considering the gradient of the total cost with respect to the parameters $\frac{\partial J}{\partial [\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}]}$, suppose the RNN processes a video and predicts a class label for every frame. Then $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}$ is a prediction for each frame, and a loss applies to each $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]$. The total cost is the sum of the losses at each timestep:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \frac{\partial J}{\partial [\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}]} = \sum_{t=0}^T \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t], \mathbf{y}_t)}{\partial [\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}]}
\end{aligned}$$

The backpropagation graph, shown in @fig-recurrent_neural_networks-bptt_J, has a branching structure. Gradients (red arrows) summate wherever the forward pass (black arrows) branches, as explained in @sec-backpropagation.

(see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN with a loss at each timestep.)
concepts.motivation_md: Backpropagation is originally defined for DAGs, but RNNs have cycles. BPTT "unrolls" the RNN into a DAG over time steps, enabling gradient computation and training of RNN parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- BPTT unrolls an RNN over $T$ timesteps to form a DAG for backpropagation.
- Exact gradients require unrolling over all timesteps; otherwise, gradients are approximations.
- Gradients for total cost sum losses at each timestep, handling branching in the computation graph.

concepts.title: The Problem of Exploding and Vanishing Gradients
concepts.one_liner: The gradient computation in RNNs can involve very long matrix products, causing gradients to explode or vanish, leading to numerical instability.
concepts.motivation_md: RNNs trained over many timesteps can have gradients that either explode or vanish due to repeated matrix multiplications, causing difficulties in learning long-range dependencies.
concepts.recap_md:
- Gradient computation in RNNs involves products of many matrices, length $\mathcal{O}(T)$.
- Large or small values in weight matrices cause gradients to explode or vanish.
- LSTM units mitigate this numerical instability problem.

key_passage.text: If values in \mathbf{W} are large, the gradient will explode. If they are small, the gradient will vanish---basically, this system is not numerically well-behaved.

motivation.text: Notice that the we can get very large computation graphs when we run an RNN for many timesteps.

example.text: Suppose we use an RNN with relu nonlinearities. Then each term \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_t}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{t-1}} equals \mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}, where \mathbf{R} is a diagonal matrix with zeros or ones on the i-th diagonal element depending on whether the i-th neuron is above or below zero at the current operating point. This gives a product \mathbf{R}_T\mathbf{W}\cdots\mathbf{R}_1\mathbf{W}. In a worst-case scenario (for numerics), suppose all the \texttt{relu} are active; then we have a product of T matrices \mathbf{W}, which means the gradient is \mathbf{W}^T (T is an exponent here, not a transpose).

This gives a product \mathbf{R}_T\mathbf{W}\cdots\mathbf{R}_1\mathbf{W}. In a worst-case scenario (for numerics), suppose all the \texttt{relu} are active; then we have a product of T matrices \mathbf{W}, which means the gradient is \mathbf{W}^T (T is an exponent here, not a transpose).

concepts.title: Long Short-Term Memory
concepts.one_liner: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units are recurrent modules designed to avoid vanishing and exploding gradients by maintaining a persistent cell state.
concepts.motivation_md: LSTMs address the vanishing and exploding gradient problems in RNNs by maintaining a persistent cell state that can store long-term information, enabling learning over long sequences.
concepts.recap_md:
- LSTMs have a cell state $\mathbf{c}$ that stores persistent memories.
- Gates decide what to forget, write, and read from the cell state.
- The cell state enables stable gradient flow and long-term memory.

key_passage.text:
(**LSTMs**) are a special kind of recurrent module, that is designed to avoid the vanishing and exploding gradients problem described in An LSTM is like a little memory controller. It has a **cell state**,
$\mathbf{c}$, which is a vector it can read from and write to. The cell
state can record memories and retrieve them as needed. The cell state
plays a similar role as the hidden state, $\mathbf{h}$, from regular
RNNs---both record memories---but the cell state is built to store
*persistent* memories that can last a long time (hence the name *long*
short-term memory).

concepts.title: forget gate
concepts.one_liner: The forget gate $\mathbf{f}_t$ decides which indices of the cell state to forget by outputting values near 0 or 1 via a sigmoid function.
concepts.motivation_md: The forget gate controls which parts of the cell state to retain or discard, enabling selective memory updating in LSTMs.
concepts.recap_md:
- The forget gate $\mathbf{f}_t$ outputs values in $[0,1]$ via sigmoid.
- Values near 1 indicate remembering; near 0 indicate forgetting.
- It modulates the cell state by pointwise multiplication.

key_passage.text:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_f\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_f) &\triangleleft \quad\quad\text{decide which indices to forget}
\end{aligned}$$ where $\mathbf{f}_t$ is a vector of length equal to the
length of the cell state $\mathbf{c}_t$, and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid
function that outputs values in the range $[0,1]$.

motivation.text:
The idea is that most
values in $\mathbf{f}_t$ will be near either $1$ (remember) or 0
(forget). Later $\mathbf{f}_t$ will be pointwise multiplied by the cell
state to forget the values where $\mathbf{f}_t$ is zero.
